expansion: The lecture defines the regurge test used in this exact scenario: "Mucopurulent discharge on compression is indicative of a patent canalicular system, but with an obstruction distal to the lower end of the lacrimal sac" (L9, slide 12). Irrigating the lower canaliculus and distending the sac, then seeing mucopurulent material reflux out of the UPPER canaliculus, therefore proves the canaliculi themselves are open and the block sits at or beyond the lacrimal sac — i.e. in the nasolacrimal duct — which in a 70-year-old with chronic tearing and discharge is the picture of chronic dacryocystitis from nasolacrimal duct obstruction. The lecture lists DCR (dacryocystorhinostomy) as the surgical treatment for acquired nasolacrimal obstruction, naming "External DCR" and "Endoscopic DCR" as the treatment options (L9, slide 29), making DCR the correct definitive treatment and matching option D. Jones I dye testing checks whether fluorescein instilled in the conjunctival sac reaches the nose through a patent system, with "Positive recovery in the nose = patent lacrimal system" and "Negative recovery... = lower duct obstruction" (L9, slide 18); since this patient has a duct-level block, Jones I would be expected to be NEGATIVE, not show dye in the nose, so option A is wrong. The reflux out of the upper canaliculus itself demonstrates that the canalicular system is patent, which the lecture's regurge-test definition directly contradicts a common canalicular obstruction (L9, slide 12) — a true canalicular block would prevent, not produce, this reflux pattern — so option B is wrong. Antibiotics can treat superimposed infection but cannot permanently cure a structural, distal outflow obstruction, which needs surgical bypass; the lecture does not present antibiotics as curative for this mechanical blockage, so option C is wrong.
objective: Recognise that upper-canaliculus reflux after lower-canaliculus irrigation indicates nasolacrimal duct obstruction requiring DCR
